body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. This game winks at another famous fantasy game in small ways, but no line may contain a name, quote, or catchphrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel. The joke is in what is there.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.
- Spoken lines are formatted: Speaker [mood]: Text   (mood optional: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary). One or two sentences a line.

THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense ("You crouch..."), or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. Never tells the player what to feel. No modern slang. When an animal speaks through the Speak with Animals spell, the Narrator reports it in quotes, in plain animal pictures (a dog says "the digger-man", "the box-maker").

CONTEXT: a long-dead, cheerful, thrifty, suspicious old pedlar who trusted no bank, no lord and no man, only his spade, buried his savings in three holes across the valley of Barovia. Each hole holds a tin and a note in his hand pointing to the next. The player found the first in a charcoal-burners' hollow above the village; its note (already written) reads: "Good health to you, friend, and to your back. A lord will tax your silver and a neighbour will borrow it till doomsday, so I put mine to bed under the pines. Take these few pieces for your trouble, since you know an honest tool when you see one. The rest of my purse sleeps where the reeds hide the lake from the road, and I keep the best of it for last. A man who trusts his spade"

HOLE 2: a reedy inlet on Lake Zarovich, hidden from the road by tall reeds: a hummock of dry ground among the reeds with a ring of stones half-sunk round it. The tin holds coins and a small healing draught and note 2, which points to hole 3: "where the old road drowns in the marsh" (the sunken causeway track into the ruined, flooded village of Berez, a witch's country).
HOLE 3: the marsh track into Berez: a slab of old road-stone at the edge of the black water, with a spade-shaped mark scratched on it. The tin holds the most coins, and his lucky spade-head (the iron blade of his first spade, worn thin), and note 3, his last: he is old now, his knees are done, this is the best of it, and the finder should keep the spade-head and use it well; a cheerful farewell.

WRITE:
1. NARRATOR, examining the hummock at the inlet before digging (two sentences, about 35 words; the turn hints it wants a spade).
2. NARRATOR, the dig at the inlet SUCCEEDS (two sentences, about 40 words).
3. NARRATOR, the dig at the inlet FAILS (one sentence, under 25 words; use {name}): water seeps into the hole as fast as it's dug.
4. NOTE 2 in the pedlar's hand (50 to 80 words), signed "A man who trusts his spade". It points to "where the old road drowns in the marsh".
5. NARRATOR, examining the slab at the marsh edge before digging (two sentences, about 35 words).
6. NARRATOR, the dig at the marsh SUCCEEDS (two sentences, about 40 words): the last tin, the spade-head.
7. NARRATOR, the dig at the marsh FAILS (one sentence, under 25 words; use {name}): black mud and the smell of the witch's country.
8. NOTE 3, his last (60 to 90 words), signed "A man who trusts his spade". Fond and a little sad; no names.

Return exactly this layout:
1A: ...
1B: ...
2A: ...
2B: ...
3A: ...
3B: ...
4A: ...
4B: ...
5A: ...
5B: ...
6A: ...
6B: ...
7A: ...
7B: ...
8A: ...
8B: ...
result:
1A: Tall reeds curtain off the carriage track, leaving only the lap of grey lake water and a dry hummock ringed with half-sunk stones. The soil between them has been turned once by an iron blade and would yield to another.
1B: Beyond the screen of rattling sedge, a mound of dry earth sits above the lake-mud inside a collar of mossy stones. Someone packed this turf down with the flat of a spade, and a spade would lift it again.
2A: The blade grates against buried tin, and you lever up a rusted box smelling of tallow and lake-damp. Inside lie silver pieces, a stoppered vial of red physic, and folded parchment kept dry in oiled linen.
2B: Threespade-depths down, the black roots part around a greased biscuit-tin wedged between two stones. It yields a handful of dry coin, a thumb-sized bottle for a strained back, and a second note written in a cramped, cheerful hand.
3A: Lake water wells up through the peat faster than {name} can fling the mud aside, turning the pit into a cold grey soup.
3B: Every spadeful {name} lifts invites two more of lake-seep, until the hole brims with reed-dirty water and refuses to give up its dead.
4A: Still digging, are you? A wet boot is a smaller sorrow than a bailiff at the door, and I left you a drop of something to warm the hinges in your spine. Take the silver and welcome. If your shoulders have another hole in them, carry your blade south to where the old road drowns in the marsh. Few folk walk there twice, which suits a careful man's savings. A man who trusts his spade
4B: You have a good eye for dry ground in a wet country, friend. Drink the little bottle if the lake-chill has got into your knees, and pocket the coin before the crows count it. The fattest part of my life's work waits down where the old road drowns in the marsh, under the noses of things too proud to look at the mud. A man who trusts his spade
5A: Here the crown of the old causeway slips under black marsh-water, save for one tilted kerb-stone scratched with the outline of a spade. The mud beneath its lip is thick as lard and has kept its shape.
5B: A slab of dressed road-stone leans at the edge of the drowned track, bearing a shallow spade-mark cut with a cold chisel. Whatever lies under it has only the frogs and the rot-weed for company.
6A: You pry the heavy mud from beneath the stone and haul up a heavy lard-tin alongside the worn iron head of an old spade. The blade is honed paper-thin by years of honest dirt, and the tin is full to the lid.
6B: Beneath the slab lies a final tallow-sealed box, resting upon the unhafted iron blade of a much-used spade. The tin clinks heavy and dull with coin, and a last sheet of parchment sits atop the silver.
7A: The trench collapses in a sigh of black bog-slime that coats {name} to the wrist with the sour reek of drowned thatch and old tallow.
7B: {name} turns up only bottomless black silt and a bubble of marsh-gas that smells of boiled cabbage and a witch's ditch.
8A: Well, friend, you have come to the bottom of my holes and the end of my thrifty years. My knees tell me the rain before it falls now, and I shall not be coming back down this track to check on my tin. Keep the coin, and take the old iron with it; it fed me forty winters and never asked for interest. Put a good ash handle to it and dig your own quiet places. Fare you well. A man who trusts his spade
8B: If you are reading this by marsh-light, you have earned every penny in the grease-tin. My digging days are done, and a man cannot take silver where I am going, nor would I trust the boatman not to weigh it short. The worn blade under the box was my first; give it a fresh haft and it will outlive us both. May your back hold out and your neighbours mind their own fences. A man who trusts his spade
